‘Never!’ the girl replied.

‘Tell me why.’

‘For one reason,’ she answered firmly, ‘that the lady knows. She will support me in it—I know she will, because she has promised. And there is another reason too. He has led a bad life, but so have I. Many of us have followed the same path together, and I won’t turn against people who could have turned against me, any one of them, but never did, bad as they are.’

‘Then,’ the gentleman said quickly, as though this was the point he had been trying to reach, ‘help me get hold of Monks, and leave me to deal with him.’

‘What if he betrays the others?’

‘I promise you that, if we force the truth from him, the matter will end there. There must be things in Oliver’s short history that would be painful to expose in public. Once we have the truth, the others will go free.’

‘And if you don’t get it?’ the girl asked.

‘Then,’ the gentleman continued, ‘Fagin will not be prosecuted without your permission. If that happens, I think I could give you reasons that would persuade you to agree.’

‘Does the lady promise that too?’ asked the girl.

‘Yes,’ Rose replied. ‘You have my solemn, honest promise.’

‘Monks would never find out how you learned what you know?’ the girl asked after a brief pause.

‘Never,’ the gentleman answered. ‘We would use the information in such a way that he could not even guess.’

‘I have been a liar, living among liars, since I was a little child,’ the girl said after another silence, ‘but I will trust your word.’

Both assured her that she could safely trust them. She then began to describe the pub from which she had been followed that night, giving its name and location. Her voice was so quiet that the listener often struggled to make out even the general meaning of her words. Her occasional pauses suggested that the gentleman was quickly writing down the information she gave him. She carefully explained the area around the pub, the best place to watch it without attracting attention, and the night and hour when Monks most often went there. Then she seemed to think for a few moments, trying to bring his face and appearance more clearly to mind.

‘He is tall,’ the girl said, ‘and strongly built, but not fat. He walks as though he is sneaking about, and he keeps looking over his shoulder, first one side, then the other.

But there was no laughter in the little town that peaceful Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s family were being dressed in mourning, amid deep grief and many tears. An unusual silence hung over the village, quiet though it generally was. People went about their business distractedly, speaking little and sighing often. Even the children seemed weighed down by the Saturday holiday. They had no enthusiasm for their games and gradually stopped playing.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself wandering sadly around the empty schoolyard. Nothing there offered her any comfort. She spoke to herself:

‘Oh, if only I had that brass knob from the fireplace stand again! Now I don’t have anything to remember him by.’ She struggled to hold back a little sob.

After a while she stopped and said to herself:

‘It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over again, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for anything in the world. But he’s gone now. I’ll never, never, never see him again.’

The thought overwhelmed her, and she wandered off with tears running down her cheeks. Soon a group of boys and girls who had played with Tom and Joe came along. They stood looking over the wooden fence and spoke solemnly about what Tom had done the last time they saw him, or some small thing Joe had said—words which, as they now easily understood, had foretold the terrible future. Each speaker pointed to the exact place where the missing boys had stood, then added something like, ‘And I was standing just like this—just as I am now, with you where he was. I was that close to him, and he smiled just this way. Then a feeling went all over me—something awful, you know. Of course I never thought what it meant then, but I understand now!’

Next they argued about who had last seen the boys alive. Many claimed that sad honour, offering evidence they had altered a little, or a great deal, to suit themselves. When they finally settled who had seen the dead boys last and spoken the last words to them, the fortunate winners took on an almost holy importance. Everyone else stared at them with envy. One poor fellow, who could think of no other claim to fame, said with fairly obvious pride in the memory:

‘Well, Tom Sawyer beat me up once.’

But his attempt to win glory failed. Most of the boys could say the same thing, so the honour was too common to count. The group drifted away, still sharing memories of the lost heroes in hushed, awed voices.

Mr. Darcy praised his sister’s accomplishments with affection.

‘I am delighted to receive so favourable an account of her,’ said Lady Catherine; ‘and please tell her from me that she must not hope to excel unless she practises a great deal.’

‘I assure you, madam,’ he answered, ‘that she has no need of that counsel. Her practice is very regular.’

‘All the better. One cannot practise too much, and in my next letter I shall urge her never to neglect it. I frequently tell young ladies that musical excellence is impossible without continual practice. I have several times informed Miss Bennet that she will never play truly well unless she practises more. And though Mrs. Collins possesses no instrument, Miss Bennet is entirely welcome, as I have often said, to visit Rosings daily and use the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. In that part of the house, you know, she would inconvenience no one.’

Mr. Darcy appeared somewhat embarrassed by his aunt’s want of manners and offered no reply.

After coffee, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth of her promise to play for him, and she immediately seated herself at the instrument. He brought a chair beside her. Lady Catherine attended to half a song before resuming her conversation with her other nephew. At length he left her and, approaching the pianoforte with his customary deliberation, placed himself where he could see the pretty performer’s face fully. Elizabeth noticed his movement and, at the first suitable pause, turned towards him with a playful smile.

‘You intend to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by approaching with such ceremony to listen. But I refuse to be alarmed, however well your sister plays. There is a stubborn part of my nature that will never submit to being frightened at another person’s pleasure. Every effort to intimidate me only increases my courage.’

‘I shall not tell you that you are wrong,’ he replied, ‘because you cannot seriously believe I have any wish to alarm you. Besides, I have enjoyed your acquaintance long enough to know how much amusement you sometimes find in expressing opinions that are not really yours.’

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this description and addressed Colonel Fitzwilliam. ‘Your cousin will furnish you with a charming idea of me, and instruct you to distrust every word I utter. How particularly unfortunate to encounter someone so capable of revealing my true character in a place where I had hoped to establish a reasonably creditable reputation.’
